options: A credential written directly into source code or a plain-text config file instead of retrieved at runtime
A secret stored in Azure Key Vault
A password that is unusually long and complex
Any variable name that contains the word "password"
questions.explain: Hardcoding means typing the actual credential value into a file that gets saved and shared, instead of fetching it from a secret store when the app runs.

questions.q: If a secret is committed to a Git repository and then removed in a later commit, what is true?
options: The secret is permanently and completely erased from the repository
Only the repository owner can ever see the old value again
Git automatically rotates any credential it detects in a diff
The secret still exists in the repository's history and can be retrieved from earlier commits
questions.explain: Deleting a line in a new commit doesn't erase it from history -- anyone who can read the repo's commit history can still retrieve the old value.

questions.q: Besides the source code file itself, where else can a hardcoded secret end up exposed?
options: CI/CD pipeline logs and container images built from that code
Nowhere -- it stays contained to the one file it was typed into
Only in the developer's local machine, never anywhere remote
Only in the compiled binary, never in logs
questions.explain: A debug step can echo the secret into build logs, and if the code ships in a container image, the secret is baked into one of that image's layers.

questions.q: Why are public GitHub repositories a particular risk for hardcoded cloud credentials?
options: GitHub deletes any file containing a password automatically
Automated scanners continuously search public repos for credential-shaped strings and can find a leak within minutes
Public repositories automatically encrypt any secrets they detect
Public repositories are not actually readable by anyone outside the organization
questions.explain: Scanning tools -- run by the platform and by independent researchers or attackers -- actively look for patterns like AWS key prefixes or Azure connection string formats.

questions.q: What is the real fix for the hardcoded-secret problem, according to this lesson?
options: Use a shorter, simpler password so it's less damaging if leaked
Retrieve the secret at runtime from a dedicated secret store instead of ever writing its value into a file
Encrypt the source code file itself with a zip password
Store the secret in a comment so developers remember to remove it
questions.explain: If the secret is never written into the file, there's nothing for Git history, CI logs, or a container image to accidentally capture.
